title: Remember me when I am gone away
short: Opening plea of a dying or departing speaker; written in 1849, when Rossetti was eighteen, and first printed in Goblin Market and Other Poems (1862).
body: The sonnet was composed in 1849 and held back for thirteen years until Rossetti's first trade volume, Goblin Market and Other Poems (1862), where it stands among the secular lyrics of the first half. The imperative 'Remember me' is a farewell formula with deep Christian resonance: the penitent thief asks Christ, 'Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom' (Luke 23:42), and the words of institution at the Eucharist ask believers to 'do this in remembrance of me'. Rossetti turns the formula toward a human beloved and then, in the sestet, questions it. 'Gone away' and 'gone far away' are euphemisms for death that the poem never names directly, a reticence characteristic of her early death lyrics.

title: the silent land
short: Death or the grave as a land of silence, a biblical idea also current through Longfellow's translation of Salis-Seewis, 'Song of the Silent Land'.
body: The Psalms repeatedly picture death as silence: 'The dead praise not the LORD, neither any that go down into silence' (Psalm 115:17); 'my soul had almost dwelt in silence' (Psalm 94:17). The phrase 'the silent land' had also become a popular nineteenth-century euphemism through Longfellow's 'Song of the Silent Land' (Voices of the Night, 1839), a translation of Johann Gaudenz von Salis-Seewis's 'Das stille Land', with its refrain 'Into the Silent Land!'. Rossetti's land is less a heaven than a place beyond communication: the speaker will be unable to hear the lover's plans or answer them. The silence links forward to the 'darkness and corruption' of the sestet and to the question of whether the dead keep any thought at all.

anchor: turn to go yet turning stay
title: half turn to go yet turning stay
short: A small dramatic picture of lovers' hesitant partings, rendered in a chiastic line that itself turns back on itself.
body: The line recalls the ordinary physical comedy of reluctant leave-taking: the speaker half turns to go, then, turning back, stays. The syntax enacts the gesture, moving 'turn ... go' and then 'turning stay', a near-chiasmus that halts the line's momentum just as the lover halts. The image is poignant because death will make this kind of reversible departure impossible: the 'going away' of line 1 is a turn that cannot be undone. Commentators often note how much of the octave consists of such remembered everyday intimacies (holding hands, talking of plans), which the speaker knows will end.

title: our future that you planned
short: The lover's talk of a shared future suggests an engagement; biographers connect the poem with Rossetti's engagement to James Collinson, though it need not be autobiographical.
body: The octave imagines a courtship in progress: the beloved talks 'day by day' of a future he has planned. Rossetti was engaged in 1848-50 to the Pre-Raphaelite painter James Collinson, an engagement broken off when he returned to Roman Catholicism, and some biographers have read the 1849 sonnet against that background. Others caution against reading Rossetti's early lyrics as confession; she was a deliberate craftswoman working in the conventions of the love sonnet. Note also the small asymmetry of 'our future that you planned': the future is shared, but the planning is his, a detail some feminist readers take as a quiet comment on the speaker's limited agency.

anchor: late to counsel then or pray
title: late to counsel then or pray
short: After death it will be too late to advise or pray; whose prayer, and for what, is left open.
body: 'Counsel' means to give or take advice, so the line closes the octave by stating that once the speaker is dead, nothing can be discussed or changed between them. 'Pray' is more ambiguous. It may mean pleading with each other (an older sense, 'I pray you'), or praying to God for the speaker's soul. Rossetti was a High Anglican shaped by the Oxford Movement, which revived interest in prayer for the dead, yet the line seems to say such prayer will come 'late', in keeping with the Protestant view that a soul's state is fixed at death. Editors leave the point open; the ambiguity sharpens the urgency of 'Only remember me' in line 7.

title: Repetition of 'remember'
short: 'Remember' sounds five times in the poem, shifting from plea in the octave to permission to forget in the sestet.
body: The word 'remember' opens lines 1 and 5, recurs in line 7, and returns in lines 10 and 14, where its meaning is reversed: the sestet allows the beloved to forget and frames remembering as a cause of sadness. The anaphora of the octave ('Remember me when ...') builds an insistent, almost liturgical cadence, while 'Only remember me' in line 7 narrows the request to its bare minimum. Critics often treat the poem's movement as a lesson in self-renunciation: the speaker gives up the claim she has so carefully pressed. The rhyme on 'understand' (l. 7) with 'land', 'hand' and 'planned' ties this narrowed plea back to the images of parting.

title: Petrarchan sonnet and volta
short: A Petrarchan sonnet (abbaabba cddece) whose volta at 'Yet' (l. 9) reverses the octave's plea.
body: The octave rhymes abbaabba on just two sounds ('away/day', 'land/hand'), an Italian discipline Rossetti, half-Italian and a reader of Dante and Petrarch, handled easily. The sestet rhymes cddece, an unusual arrangement that delays the final rhyme of 'smile' with 'while' (l. 9) until line 13 and keeps the closing line, 'sad', echoing 'had' (l. 12). The turn comes, in the classical place, with 'Yet' at line 9: the speaker concedes that forgetting is permissible and even preferable. Unlike Shakespeare's sonnets, there is no closing couplet, but lines 13-14 work as an antithetical pair ('forget and smile' / 'remember and be sad').

title: darkness and corruption
short: Biblical language for the decay of the body in the grave.
body: 'Corruption' is the standard Authorized Version word for bodily decay after death: 'neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption' (Psalm 16:10, quoted in Acts 2:27), and Paul's 'It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption' (1 Corinthians 15:42). Darkness and the grave are coupled in Job (e.g. 10:21-22, 'the land of darkness and the shadow of death'). Rossetti's phrase thus places the speaker's body firmly in the grave, yet the conditional 'if' (l. 11) leaves open whether any part of the mind survives there. For a Christian reader the Pauline context also implies a future resurrection beyond the decay the line describes.

title: vestige
short: A trace or remnant; from Latin vestigium, a footprint.
body: A 'vestige' is what remains of something that has otherwise disappeared, a trace or mark. The Latin vestigium literally means the sole of the foot or a footprint, so the word carries a faint image of a track left behind by someone who has gone away, quietly echoing 'gone away' in lines 1-2. The speaker imagines the possibility that a trace of her former thoughts might survive the grave's 'darkness and corruption', and specifically her thought of loving the beloved. The precise, almost scientific Latinate word contrasts with the plain monosyllables of the octave and marks the intellectual hesitation of the sestet.

anchor: the thoughts that once I had
title: Do the dead remember?
short: Whether the dead keep any consciousness is left uncertain; critics link this to Rossetti's interest in 'soul sleep' between death and resurrection.
body: The sestet doubts whether any 'vestige' of thought survives death. Jerome McGann argued that the idea of 'soul sleep' (psychopannychism), the belief that the soul rests unconscious or dreaming until the Last Judgement, is a central enabling principle of Rossetti's religious poetry, and many of her lyrics present the dead as sleeping and oblivious. Antony Harrison and later critics qualify this, noting that Rossetti treats the state as a brief interval and varies her imagery from poem to poem. Ecclesiastes offers a biblical basis for the doubt: 'the dead know not any thing ... for the memory of them is forgotten' (9:5). The uncertainty makes the speaker's final generosity more striking: she cannot know whether she will mind being forgotten.

title: Better ... forget and smile
short: The poem ends by preferring the beloved's happiness to the speaker's memory, a reversal of the octave's plea.
body: The final antithesis, 'forget and smile' against 'remember and be sad', resolves the sonnet in favour of the living. The renunciation has a famous precedent in Shakespeare's Sonnet 71 ('No longer mourn for me when I am dead'), where the speaker would rather be forgotten than cause grief; Rossetti's poem is often read alongside it. Readers differ on its tone. Some find selfless love; others hear a muted reproach, or the self-effacement expected of Victorian women; still others see Christian detachment from earthly attachment. The modest phrase 'Better by far' keeps the ending gentle rather than heroic, and the poem's last word, 'sad', lingers despite the consolation.
